Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a court may consider documents incorporated by reference into the complaint on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion without converting it into a summary judgment motion.

Cite at least six decisions of the Ninth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. THE DISTRICT COURT PROPERLY CONSIDERED DOCUMENTS INCORPORATED BY REFERENCE IN THE COMPLAINT WITHOUT CONVERTING THE RULE 12(b)(6) MOTION INTO ONE FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT.

Rule 12(d) requires conversion to summary judgment only when "matters outside the pleadings are presented to and not excluded by the court." Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(d). This Court has long held that documents incorporated by reference in the complaint are not "outside the pleadings." A court "may . . . consider certain materials—documents attached to the complaint, documents incorporated by reference in the complaint, or matters of judicial notice—without converting the motion to dismiss into a motion for summary judgment." *United States v. Ritchie*, 342 F.3d 903, 908 (9th Cir. 2003). Review of that determination is de novo as to whether the document qualified for consideration. *See id.* at 907–08.

**A. The incorporation-by-reference doctrine is well settled.**

"Even if a document is not attached to a complaint, it may be incorporated by reference into a complaint if the plaintiff refers extensively to the document or the document forms the basis of the plaintiff's claim." *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 907. This Court has long permitted consideration of documents "whose contents are alleged in a complaint and whose authenticity no party questions, but which are not physically attached to the plaintiff's pleading." *In re Silicon Graphics Inc. Sec. Litig.*, 183 F.3d 970, 986 (9th Cir. 1999) (citation omitted), *abrogated on other grounds by S. Ferry LP, No. 2 v. Killinger*, 542 F.3d 776, 784 (9th Cir. 2008); *accord Branch v. Tunnell*, 14 F.3d 449, 454 (9th Cir. 1994), *overruled on other grounds by Galbraith v. County of Santa Clara*, 307 F.3d 1119, 1127 (9th Cir. 2002).

The Court has framed the inquiry as a three-part test. A court may consider evidence on which the complaint "necessarily relies" if "(1) the complaint refers to the document; (2) the document is central to the plaintiff's claim; and (3) no party questions the authenticity of the copy attached to the 12(b)(6) motion." *Marder v. Lopez*, 450 F.3d 445, 448 (9th Cir. 2006) (citation omitted). The doctrine also reaches cases in which "the plaintiff's claim depends on the contents of a document, the defendant attaches the document to its motion to dismiss, and the parties do not dispute the authenticity of the document, even though the plaintiff does not explicitly allege the contents of that document in the complaint." *Knievel v. ESPN*, 393 F.3d 1068, 1076 (9th Cir. 2005). *See also Coto Settlement v. Eisenberg*, 593 F.3d 1031, 1038 (9th Cir. 2010) (court may consider documents incorporated by reference without converting the motion).

**B. The doctrine prevents selective pleading.**

The doctrine rests on fairness. It "prevents plaintiffs from selecting only portions of documents that support their claims, while omitting portions of those very documents that weaken—or doom—their claims." *Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc.*, 899 F.3d 988, 1002 (9th Cir. 2018). A plaintiff cannot avoid dismissal by quoting or relying on a document in part while keeping the rest of it from the court. *See Silicon Graphics*, 183 F.3d at 986; *Knievel*, 393 F.3d at 1076.

**C. The documents here satisfy the doctrine.**

[Defendant should conform this section to the record.] The Complaint expressly refers to the [identify document(s)], *see* [ER __, Compl. ¶¶ __], and Plaintiff's [identify claim] depends on their contents. They are therefore "central" to the claim, *Marder*, 450 F.3d at 448, and form its "basis," *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 907. Plaintiff never questioned their authenticity below. *See* [ER __]. Consideration of the documents therefore did not require conversion under Rule 12(d). *See Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908.

**D. The district court used the documents within the doctrine's limits.**

Defendant acknowledges that the doctrine has limits. Although a court may consider an incorporated document, "it is improper to assume the truth of an incorporated document if such assumptions only serve to dispute facts stated in a well-pleaded complaint." *Khoja*, 899 F.3d at 1003. The district court did not cross that line. It considered the documents for what they say, not to resolve factual disputes against Plaintiff. *See id.* at 1002–03; *see also Lee v. City of Los Angeles*, 250 F.3d 668, 688–90 (9th Cir. 2001) (distinguishing consideration of a document's existence and contents from acceptance of disputed facts within it). Where, as here, the complaint's own allegations are contradicted by the incorporated document's terms, the court need not accept as true allegations that the document itself refutes. *See Sprewell v. Golden State Warriors*, 266 F.3d 979, 988 (9th Cir. 2001) (court need not accept as true allegations contradicted by documents referred to in the complaint).

Because the challenged documents were referenced in the Complaint, were central to Plaintiff's claim, and were undisputedly authentic, the district court properly considered them without converting the motion. This Court should affirm.
